messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Karim al-Mansour, a 38-year-old American of Lebanese descent living alone, had spent the better part of the last year retreating from a world that suddenly felt fundamentally unsafe. Six months prior, a severe autoimmune crisis had plunged him into a critical care unit where every breath felt borrowed. The hospitalization was defined by the relentless intrusion of medical procedures: nurses adjusting his central line, the sharp pinch of diagnostic taps against his abdomen, and the constant, invasive monitoring that stripped him of autonomy. Photographs from that time captured his hollowed face next to coiled tubes and sterile drapes, images that now sat on his phone’s locked screen, untouched and heavy. When the trauma subsided and he returned to his daily life, the salon he had run for a decade became a landscape of landmines. It was during his second week back, wiping down his station after a client left, that the first fracture appeared. A routine tube of antiseptic hand gel caught his eye, and the visual of its white cap instantly triggered a violent physical reactivity. His breath hitched, his heart hammered against his ribs, and a wave of horror and shame flooded his chest. His body was on alert, coiled tight and ready to flee, as if the danger were still in the room. This sudden physiological storm did not stop at his skin. It pulled him directly into the memory of the ward. Just as quickly, an olfactory recall washed over him—the sharp, chemical tang of the salon’s floor cleaner morphing in his mind into the sterile, copper scent of the hospital corridors. The association was immediate and inescapable. As the memory took hold, pain recall struck; the exact pressure he felt during the intubation brace throbbed in his sternum, stripping away any context and leaving only emotion without image, a raw, nameless dread that his body was failing him. The initial flood of sensations quickly hardened into a rigid set of beliefs. Karim had come to view his own physiology as an enemy, a traitor that kept reacting as if he were still in the ICU even when he was safe on his couch. This conviction that his body was utterly unreliable bred a quiet, gnawing fear that he was going crazy. The appraisal that his mind was fracturing did not remain passive. It fed his threat system, amplifying his negative emotions until his baseline state was one of constant bodily tension. He walked through his days with his shoulders braced, his jaw clenched, convinced that any sudden spike in anxiety was proof of his unraveling. This internal distrust did not merely sit in his head; it actively shaped what he noticed. His belief that he could no longer trust his internal signals made him hyper-vigilant to environmental cues, instantly dialing his threat response to a fever pitch. When a friend texted to say, “I heard you’re seeing a doctor again,” the phrase acted as a trigger, instantly reinforcing his appraisal that his body was a broken system. His body surged with physical reactivity, his palms sweating and his vision tunneling, mirroring the exact physiological cascade he experiences during procedures. The cycle tightened over the following months, calcifying into a pattern that severed him from his work and his community. Avoidance became a reflex. He stopped answering shift requests, telling the salon owner he was taking a sabbatical, though he knew it was a retreat from the fear of losing control. He avoided grocery stores, canceled his dentist appointment, and kept a bottle of water on his nightstand to ground himself when he woke from a nightmare, the dream residue leaving him gasping and convinced the crisis was returning. Yet, the more he tried to suppress his reactions, the more power the memories held. The memory of his hospitalization became a magnet for his fear. When the memory returned, the emotional intensity stripped away context, flooding his system with immediate threat. It didn’t just cause physical reactivity; it pulled him directly toward medical triggers. He found himself searching hospital forums, his phone screen lit by the blue glow of patient diagrams, unable to look away. This compulsive checking only fed his threat perception. The sustained mental focus on his symptoms kept his nervous system in a permanent state of alarm, which in turn pulled him deeper into the memory of his illness. Each spike of negative emotions and bodily tension validated his core belief, creating a seamless loop where fear and memory constantly reinforced the sensation of threat. Now, Karim sits in the quiet waiting room of a community clinic, his hands knotted in his lap. The hair clips and shears that once defined his identity gather dust on a shelf at home, a concrete monument to a life put on hold. What finally brought him through the door was a panic attack in his shower, where the spray pattern perfectly mimicked the mist of his nebulizer treatments, pushing him to acknowledge that isolation was not protecting him. He is terrified that the therapist will see him as fundamentally broken, that the machinery beneath his skin is permanently fractured. What he hopes for, with a fragile certainty, is simply to stop bracing for a collapse that no longer exists, to believe that his pulse is a rhythm and not a warning, and to return to his chair without feeling like he is standing on an operating table.
